summary:
LUMEN is an interactive lunar landing site screening platform engineered to help mission planners, educators, and the public evaluate surface lighting and Earth visibility conditions across candidate lunar landing sites. 

At the lunar South Pole, grazing solar elevation angles and Earth’s libration wobble create extreme environmental swings where minor arrival slips can plunge a surface mission into prolonged darkness. LUMEN addresses the "Lunar Landing Site Navigator" challenge by coupling deterministic NASA NAIF SPICE ephemeris calculations with an intuitive mission control interface. Users can track Sun and Earth azimuth/elevation, inspect refined rise and set countdowns across a 60-day timeline, compare two landing sites simultaneously, and evaluate schedule slips in seconds. 

By making the operational consequences of launch delays visible before flight commitments, LUMEN transforms complex astrodynamic ephemerides into accessible, actionable screening insights.
details:
LUMEN (Lunar Landing Site Navigator)

1. What It Does & How It Works

LUMEN (Lunar Landing Site Navigator) provides deterministic geometric screening of surface solar illumination (power and thermal context) and direct line-of-sight visibility to Earth (geometric direct-to-Earth communications) across candidate lunar landing sites:

  • Surface-Observer Topocentric Geometry: Sun and Earth positions are calculated relative to physical surface coordinates on the Moon rather than the lunar center, accounting for the critical ~0.26° angular parallax that directly impacts horizon clearance.
  • High-Resolution 60-Day Architecture: Precomputed at 15-minute intervals across 2027-01-01T00:00:00Z to 2027-03-02T00:00:00Z using NAIF SPICE planetary ephemerides and the explicit DE440 lunar body-fixed frame (MOON_ME_DE440_ME421).
  • Interactive Mission Control: Features a responsive 3D lunar limb with real-time solar illumination angles, a local East-North-Up (ENU) sky dome, apparent elevation/azimuth gauges, and sub-minute refined event countdowns (next sunrise, sunset, Earthrise, Earthset).
  • The Schedule Slip Engine: Allows planners to evaluate launch slips by selecting two distinct arrival dates for any polar site; the engine instantly recalculates 7-day landing slices to reveal shifts in dark runs and communications outages.
  • Compare Mode: Simultaneously visualizes two lunar sites side-by-side using a single synchronized time cursor.
  • Live Ephemeris Context: Connects to the NASA/JPL Horizons API for real-time orbital context and current-minute celestial vectors, maintained separately from the precomputed mission series.

2. Benefits & Intended Impact

Landing site selection is among the highest-risk phases of lunar exploration, particularly at the lunar South Pole where low solar incidence angles (axial tilt ~1.54°) and Earth’s libration wobble create extreme localized environmental swings. Existing astrodynamics software (e.g., JPL Horizons, Quickmap) is built primarily for orbital specialists and involves steep learning curves:

  • Rapid Sensitivity Screening: Planners can assess operational trade-offs and "what-if" launch delays in seconds.
  • Mission Risk Reduction: Demonstrates immediately whether a delayed arrival causes power starvation (e.g., plunging Malapert Massif into 168 hours of continuous dark during a 30-day schedule slip).
  • Public & Educational Accessibility: Translates complex topocentric ephemerides into an intuitive, tactile tool for educators, students, and space enthusiasts.

3. Tools, Technologies & Super Intelligence (AI) Integration

Our team paired industry-standard engineering stacks with a multi-agent Super Intelligence (AI) workflow to maximize productivity and rigor:

  • Scientific Computing Engine: Python 3.12, SpiceyPy (NAIF SPICE toolkit wrapper), NumPy.
  • Frontend & 3D Visualization: TypeScript, React 19, Three.js, React Three Fiber (@react-three/fiber), Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lenis, and GSAP.
  • Validation Infrastructure: NASA/JPL Horizons API and automated Python/Vitest test suites.
  • Deployment: Vercel edge infrastructure with serverless same-origin proxy routes.

Super Intelligence (AI/SI) Development Workflow:

The solution idea, scientific scope, and engineering constraints were conceived and directed entirely by the human team (The Black Bulls). AI tools were strategically deployed as specialized accelerators across distinct lifecycle phases:

  • Anthropic Claude: Assisted during initial sprint planning, task breakdown, architectural mapping, and structuring interface requirements.
  • Google Gemini: Utilized for deep technical research, analyzing NASA NAIF kernel frame documentation, and synthesizing cited coordinate literature for Artemis landing candidate sites.
  • OpenAI Codex: Served as a productivity accelerator for scaffolding TypeScript components, implementing reactive state hooks (Zustand), and preparing unit test coverage.
  • Google Antigravity: Managed end-to-end browser automation, high-resolution UI scene recordings, 1080p video production, and slide deck packaging.

4. Creativity & Innovation

  • Treating Schedule Variation as a Primary Variable: Rather than showing isolated single-epoch views, LUMEN focuses on the operational reality of spaceflight—schedule slips—turning static ephemeris data into dynamic contingency planning.
  • Unified Time Synchronization: A single, continuous time cursor simultaneously updates the 3D Moon lighting, the local ENU sky dome, numerical telemetry gauges, and side-by-side comparison panels.
  • Tactile Narrative Design: Combines cinematic landing storytelling with a dense, trust-building scientific workbench.

5. Critical Engineering Factors & Transparency

  • Deterministic Science First: AI tools were strictly barred from generating astrodynamic figures. All geometry is calculated deterministically via SPICE and independently cross-checked against NASA/JPL Horizons observer tables (max angular deviation < 0.005°, event times within 58 seconds).
  • Geometric Screening Honesty: LUMEN calculates geometric line of sight over a flat reference sphere horizon. The interface transparently states that real terrain is not modeled in v1, and that geometric Earth visibility does not constitute an RF communications link budget.
  • Compliance: No NASA logos, flags, or mission identifiers were created or altered using AI tools.
